devpost_page.title: μTeX (MuTeX)
devpost_page.tagline: μTeX turns math equations on blackboards into LaTeX for easy notetaking. LaTeX is an accessible tool for blind individuals to read math. Combined with TTS, μTeX is an inclusive solution to learn math.

sections.text: μTeX: A LaTeX Transcription Tool Pronounced Mew-tech. (MuTeX)

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: μTeX is my two loves of my life combined: chalkboard and LaTeX. However, that does not mean I am the fastest LaTeX writer. I always aspired to be that student who writes math notes in LaTeX, but my slow typing (66 wpm: embarrassing for a CS major) limits my dreams. I needed some external help for accurate LaTeX math notes. Thinking about my love for LaTeX, I remembered an essay I wrote for an English class about LaTeX. I wrote about how my professor refuses to give LaTeX source code for our homework, and why he should start doing so. One thing I learned at that time was LaTeX's accessibility. ... characteristics of standardized syntax across LaTeX users “...allow the blind user to access some mainstream mathematical resources on the web. … If a blind person reads the formulas on this page with a screen reader, she/he will hear their LaTeX representations.” (Maneki and Jeans) Verbally reading mathematical expressions is challenging, and LaTeX provides a standard tool. Then I questioned, how does a blackboard-based math class scene translate to blind individuals? With this question and my struggles writing LaTeX notes, I decided to create μTeX.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: μTeX is a web-based application that transcribes handwritten math equations from blackboards into LaTeX syntax. μTeX uses the Gemini library to recognize math equations in real-time. Live camera captures the user's view, which is then fed into Gemini with a prompt. The output is a clean LaTeX script for easy integration into notes, papers, or digital documents. A key feature is accessibility: LaTeX is accessible, and it provides real-time assistance in equation interpretation for blind and/or visually impaired individuals. TTS is available, which lets blind and visually impaired individuals engage with math content independently. The platform supports both casual users and academic institutions aiming for more inclusive education. Overall, it bridges the gap between traditional math instruction and modern, accessible digital workflows.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: I used plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for this project. I like the simple, old-style websites that are easy to navigate. The Gemini API was used for OCR and the browser's TTS.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: I initially planned to deploy the project via GitHub, but encountered a limitation: using plain JavaScript made it difficult to secure the API key without exposing it. Rather than compromising security, I chose to prioritize improving the core functionality of the product. I believe that building a strong, feature-rich foundation is more important at this stage. Deployment can be addressed later using a more suitable environment like Node.js, where secure key management is easier to implement.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: This is my first time solo-hacking, and I had to start late with limited resources (me and myself). I was able to create a functional product that I am passionate about, hence my two loves combined. I am proud of the hours I put into making μTeX work and keep trying despite the absence of teammates.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: I think out of all things I learned, the most important lesson was making products accessible. Balancing features with user needs is crucial, and inclusive technology can help everyone in the community.

sections.heading: What's next for μTeX (MuTeX)
sections.text: Increased accuracy in transcription, deployment, live LaTeX compilation for visual accuracy checking, and volume and speed control for TTS

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Vouch began with three experiences in the days before Cal Hacks. At the airport before his flight to the hackathon, Shubhay tried to resolve an order issue and found that requesting his refund required him to submit a written request followed by a call. Shivam spoke with a single father living paycheck to paycheck who had several hundred dollars tied up in a refund for weeks and his repeated follow-ups brought only "verification pending." Aadi was exploring an agent to simplify airline-ticket refunds and became familiar with the trend towards development of agents to complete these tasks. Together, these experiences made us ask what personal finance will look like when agents can buy, document problems, and request refunds for us. We decided that merchants need a signal they can trust while consumers needed a faster way to verify. We chose refunds as a focused starting point: simplify the consumer's work while helping merchants detect fraudulent claims, coordinated abuse, and scalping behavior as agent-driven commerce grows. The stakes already exist: Appriss Retail's research with Deloitte estimated $103 billion in U.S. losses from fraudulent returns and claims in 2024 , while NRF's 2025 survey found 71% of consumers were less likely to return to a retailer after a poor returns experience . When the investigation supports approval, Vouch immediately submits the refund recommendation into the merchant's decision workflow; recommendations to reject go to the company for human review rather than automatically denying the customer. sections.text: Giving agents useful tools within enforceable limits. Droid's tool behavior differed between autonomy settings, and script batches required inspecting their nested calls. We built explicit permission checks and recovery messages so a refused operation did not silently end an otherwise useful investigation. Handling asynchronous and imperfect agent outputs. CREAO runs can take minutes, and live responses do not always match the expected structure. sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: As technology students, long study sessions and late-night coding make it easy to forget how we’re sitting. We wanted to make posture awareness part of everyday desk life, with clear feedback and encouragement from friends. That idea became pose.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Pose pairs a posture-tracking wearable with a web dashboard and leaderboard. Users can review their history, create friend groups, and compete in weekly rankings based on the percentage of tracked time spent slouching. The most-improved member is highlighted and celebrates personal progress among a group.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We developed firmware for an ESP32 and BNO055 sensor, keeping calibration, posture classification, and episode timing on the wearable. Bluetooth Low Energy sends calculated results to the browser. Ruby on Rails handles accounts, saved sessions, and group rankings. Tiger Data’s PostgreSQL, hypertable, and TimescaleDB support session storage and snapshot history.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Connecting hardware, Bluetooth, and persistent storage required careful coordination. We had to distinguish brief movement from sustained slouching, prevent repeated uploads from double-counting activity, and show when readings became stale or disconnected. Another challenge was making the dashboard useful without overwhelming users with measurements.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We built firmware, browser Bluetooth integration, authenticated storage, and a social dashboard around a shared data contract. We’re especially proud of combining friendly competition with recognition for individual improvement. Automated tests cover timing, upload handling, and account isolation; physical end-to-end verification remains a next step.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Reliable wearable experiences depend on more than sensor readings. Calibration, connection failures, data consistency, and clear feedback all shape whether users can trust what they see. We also learned to distinguish live posture from sustained episodes and to measure progress only against recorded tracking time.

sections.text: As outdoor enthusiasts and avid hikers the idea of off trail wilderness adventure has long been attractive. Traveling cross country requires meticulous planning as one miscalculation can lead to disaster. To this end we have created OffTrails, a wilderness route selection aide which seeks to maximize the safety, efficiency, and speed of cross country travel.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: The program pulls topological data from the US Geological Survey and water/vegetation data from ESA's Sentinel-2 L2A satellite. After allowing the user to provide the desired start and end point of their route, the program runs a modified A* pathfinding algorithm on the data taking the multitude of factors into account. The resulting route will then be displayed in the WebUI and a route GPX file can be downloaded into the user's preferred map app at their convenience.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built a web interface using leaflet. The backend code is written in python and uses various standard python analytics packages (matplotlib, numpy, etc.) as well as some geography specific packages such as rasterio and gpxpy. Our A* pathfinding algorithm makes use of a cost function that represents the difficulty of each terrain segment in question. Initially this cost function was implemented using Tobler's Hiking Formula but was replaced by a more accurate model published in Minetti et al. (2002), Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes . AI was used to greatly optimize this formula so it could be run under the time constraints of a user application.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Integrating different geographical datasets. Tuning constants for the pathfinding algorithm.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Retrieving geographical data from various sources. Designing a multifaceted pathfinding algorithm that achieves the project goals.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Global Information System analysis and processing. Advanced routefinding algorithms and cost function selection Developing software under tight time constraints

sections.heading: What's next for OffTrails
sections.text: In the future we would like to implement a hierarchical path finding algorithm which would involve multiple passes of path finding algorithms at increasingly high map resolutions. This approach could allow for great improvement in search radius and program efficiency, as well as have smoother and more accurate trails. We would also like to implement a larger search area, and find a good solution to deal with the huge files that come with working with geographic information system data.

devpost_page.title: Cropora - Field Intelligence Platform
devpost_page.tagline: Know your fields before the season starts.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Agriculture runs on uncertainty. Farmers commit to seeds and inputs months before they know what the season will bring. Lenders underwrite crop loans without knowing what is actually in the ground. Cropora was built to close that information gap using eleven years of satellite data that already exists and is largely underutilized at the field level.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Cropora is a field intelligence platform for Iowa cropland built on three public satellite datasets spanning 2013 to 2023. It does four things: analyzes crop-specific NDVI phenology for corn and soybean across the growing season; classifies every Iowa cropland pixel into regular rotation, monoculture, or irregular using eleven years of USDA CDL data; trains two Random Forest models for crop type prediction (78% accuracy using NDVI features alone, 96% using CDL history); and projects the 2024 crop type for every field with a pixel-level confidence score. All of this feeds into a Field Resilience Score, a composite 0-100 metric combining rotation consistency, crop diversity, and recent stability, giving lenders and agronomists a single actionable number before planting season begins.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Three Python notebooks in Colab, one per analytical task, with a Streamlit dashboard for the final interface. CDL rasters were downloaded via the USDA CropScape API for all eleven years. NDVI composites came from NASA AppEEARS (MOD13Q1.061) and soil moisture from SMAP L4 (SPL4SMGP.008). All datasets were reprojected and spatially aligned using rasterio. The dashboard uses Streamlit and Plotly with an interactive Iowa region map, a what-if rotation threshold slider, and a field intelligence lookup with plain-English lending recommendations per region.

sections.heading: Challenges ran into
sections.text: The eleven-year CDL stack at native 30m resolution produced an array nearly 4.7GB in memory, crashing Colab repeatedly. Downsampling to 300m using rasterio reduced the stack to 47MB while preserving the rotation signal at agronomically meaningful resolution. The CropScape API also required bounding boxes in EPSG:5070 rather than WGS84, a silent failure mode that cost significant debugging time.

sections.heading: Accomplishments
sections.text: 96% accuracy on the CDL history model with a nearly diagonal confusion matrix, and a predicted 2023 crop map visually indistinguishable from CDL ground truth. The Field Resilience Score synthesizes three independent satellite data streams into one number that a non-technical lender or insurer can actually act on.

sections.heading: What was learned
sections.text: Geospatial preprocessing takes longer than the modeling. The 18-point accuracy gap between the NDVI-only model and the CDL history model was the most interesting finding: agronomic memory, what a field grew last year and the year before, is the dominant signal for predicting what it will grow next. Single-season satellite imagery is informative but incomplete.

sections.text: Etika: Legal Team, Decoded. A friend spent a whole weekend trying to figure out if her candle business needed to register for PST. Four government sites, a Reddit thread, and a phone call later, the answer was "not yet, but close." Compliance info isn't missing, it's fragmented. BizPaL lists permits that may apply, Ownr just registers a name, and an accountant only knows what you tell them. Nobody says what applies to you , why, and what to do next, and the thresholds move underneath you the whole time. So we built Etika.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Etika is a compliance navigator for new Vancouver sole proprietors. You answer a few questions and confirm the facts Etika understood. Three specialist AI agents (Registration, Tax, and Employer, each with its own persona) then check your situation against official government sources. You get a readiness score, plain-English explanations with the official government source behind each one, and a Now/Next/Later plan where every item links to the real form. Mention a change in chat, like "I'm hiring next month," and Etika proposes a fact update. Confirm it and the assessment re-runs live: the employer obligations (WorkSafeBC, CRA payroll account, minimum wage, pay statements, payroll records) move from Later to Now, and the score updates with them.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic v2 Database: TiDB Cloud, holding vectors and relational data in one store AI: Gemini Flash for intake parsing, agent explanations and chat; gemini-embedding-001 for retrieval Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind The core rule is code decides, Gemini explains. Every profile fact is stored as a value plus a confirmed flag, and an unknown fact is never treated as "no." Skip a question and the requirement becomes "Needs your input," not a guess. A deterministic engine matches confirmed facts against a reviewed registry of requirements, each tagged now, trigger or recommendation, with dependencies (business number before GST or payroll). Tax calculators run the real tests: PST's rolling 12-month $10,000 small-seller line plus the no-premises condition, GST's $30,000 threshold, and a straight-line projection of when you'll cross each one. The score and the order of next steps come from the same code, never from the model. The knowledge base is ours. We collected official BC Registries, CRA, WorkSafeBC, BC Laws and City of Vancouver pages by hand, split them by legal section, embedded them, and stored them in TiDB with metadata for authority, jurisdiction, requirement and retrieval date. Every chunk has a review status, and only approved chunks can be retrieved. Retrieval is filtered by requirement and jurisdiction, and returns "insufficient evidence" instead of a weak match. Each agent owns one area of the registry, receives only the evide

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: The law was harder than the code. PST's exemption depends on a rolling window, not a calendar year, so one good month can flip your status, and it also depends on whether you have established premises, which market sales make ambiguous. We flag those cases as gray areas for a professional instead of resolving them. Building the knowledge base from scratch was the other big job. The hardest part wasn't collecting pages, it was narrowing each agent enough that it could only answer from its evidence, so Gemini never filled a gap with something that sounded right but wasn't sourced. Three parallel agents also blew through Gemini's rate limit fast. We rebuilt the pipeline so code prefetches all evidence up front and each agent makes exactly one call, cutting Gemini usage from 8 to 15 requests per assessment down to 3.

sections.heading: What we're proud of
sections.text: The RAG pipeline: we built the whole source-to-citation process ourselves, from scraping and reviewing official sources to chunking, embedding, and gating retrieval so an agent can only cite evidence it actually pulled in that run. Because status comes from code, the same facts always produce the same score, and the model can't talk its way into a different answer. And the hiring moment, one sentence in chat and several legal obligations switching on live, is the best 10 seconds of the demo.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Pre-filled government forms generated from the saved profile, auto-generated policy documents (privacy, refund, workplace), a renewal and deadline calendar, and expansion beyond Vancouver sole proprietors to other BC cities and business structures.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Egg prices over the last few years made it obvious to everyone: diseases like avian influenza move through commercial flocks incredibly fast , killing birds in the hundreds of thousands. By the time a farmer notices something is wrong, the disease may already have swept through an entire house. That disrupts farms, cuts the egg supply, and drives up prices for everyone. So we asked: how can we give farmers an early warning system that: watches the flock constantly , for long periods, keeps working when the internet drops or part of the system crashes, and turns what it sees into something a farmer and a veterinarian can actually act on ?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Henomaly is a camera-based edge AI system running on QNX that monitors the relative health of different groups of chickens. Instead of streaming video to the cloud, it processes everything locally , because barn internet is anything but reliable. It watches behavior (inactivity, panting, eating, drinking, movement) and looks for visible changes in droppings . When something is unusual, it creates an alert with the pen, the time, an evidence image , and an explanation of what changed . The alert reaches the farmer through Photon and iMessage . The farmer can ask questions, request the image, and decide whether to share it with a veterinarian. Nothing is automatically diagnosed, and nothing is escalated without the farmer's permission.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The edge: QNX 8 on a Raspberry Pi 5 The core system runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with QNX 8.0 and a Camera Module 3 . Nine separate processes , each with one job and its own priority, talking over native QNX message passing . Large camera frames move through shared memory instead of being copied between processes. The camera is driven through QNX's Sensor Framework in C. Full-resolution frames land in a shared-memory ring that other processes read without copying, protected by a sequence counter. Only small summaries travel as messages. Real-time priorities: the camera and the farmer's alert link run at the highest priority, and heavy model inference runs at the lowest. Inference can never starve an alert. On-device AI from QNX's open-source ecosystem: ONNX Runtime 1.24.4 from oss.qnx.com , installed completely offline (106 packages, no internet on the Pi). sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Making a language-model platform train vision models. Veri's sandboxed containers originally had only 64 MB of shared memory , which crashed PyTorch's data-loading workers and multi-GPU training. We patched the DataLoader to pass batches through pipes as NumPy arrays , keeping 12 data workers per GPU alive. We reported the cap with logs , and the Veri team raised it to 16 GB, which unlocked multi-GPU training. We also reported custom scripts failing on one GPU provider and a crash about 20 minutes into jobs, and Veri shipped fixes during the event . Expensive failures. A job marked "failed" made even its finished models undownloadable, so we made our training jobs: time-boxed , sizing training to the remaining budget, always exit cleanly , so trained models survive, check multi-GPU communication in 10 seconds before paying for a 30-minute download, and resubmit automatically through GPU capacity and quota errors. Data at scale on bad Wi-Fi. Downloading 33 GB of video inside cloud jobs stalled, so we moved video processing to a laptop and uploaded only the compact prepared dataset. QNX packaging. The ONNX Runtime package had to be installed offline, and its broken Python binding forced us to call the C API directly.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A full edge AI pipeline on QNX : camera, detection, alerts and a self-healing supervisor, running on a Raspberry Pi 5 with no cloud dependency . Models trained end-to-end on Veri , including multi-GPU training, on a platform designed for language models. Honest numbers : every score is on held-out data, split by video, not by frame. A working farmer loop : alerts with evidence over iMessage, with the farmer in control of what reaches the vet. Real contributions back : a drafted fix for QNX's ONNX Runtime package, and platform bugs reported to Veri that were fixed during the event.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: The most important lesson was where our models do not work . Our droppings model performed well on close-up photos but failed on distant, crowded barn footage . On real held-out pen frames, 0 of its 34 detections were actually droppings : they landed on feathers, dye marks, wall screws and drinker parts. A synthetic benchmark had suggested it worked; only a check on real held-out footage showed it didn't. Even at full 2688-px resolution, individual droppings weren't visible. So instead of hiding it, we changed the design : Wide cameras handle flock-level behavior, where our models are validated on exactly that kind of footage. Droppings analysis needs a closer, controlled camera position. In the demo we simulate that path: after the dropping-finding step, the close-up analysis model receives droppings we'd expect from that camera position, at the simulated anomaly level. We also learned that honest evaluation is a design tool : splitting by video, scoring on held-out data, and auditing real frames changed our architecture more than any extra training would have.

devpost_page.tagline: Your hands-free conversational survival assistant. Powered by on device LLM inference, offering step-by-step instructions to keep you smarter and safer anytime, anywhere.

sections.text: SurviveX Link to demo

sections.heading: The Problem 💭
sections.text: 30% of people who get lost in the wilderness never find their way back. Imagine yourself lost and alone in the middle of nowhere, no internet access to call for help or look up survival knowledge and time is running out . Whether it's a hiker with a broken leg, a soldier in combat, a responder during a natural disaster, or someone lost at sea, the lack of internet connectivity and immediate expert guidance can mean the difference between life or death .

sections.heading: Our Solution ⚙️
sections.text: SurviveX is an offline embedded AI assistant that combines Edge AI on a hands free device like the Apple Vision Pro along with health monitoring and voice guidance to provide real-time survival assistance . Our assistant provides step-by-step guidance , offering stressed users fast responses and ample opportunity for clarification throughout the process. Tracking vital signs through Terra's API , using them to augment our responses. Our machine learning model is designed to run on a hands free device like the Apple Vision Pro enabling survivors, first responders and soldiers to communicate via speech so your hands can focus on what matters : survival . Fine tuning our model to provide a user specific solution governed by environment indicative of the stress of the situation. Whether you need to treat an injury, start a fire with flint, fix up your broken car on the side of the highway, or aimlessly wonder and be navigated by the stars. SurviveX acts as your personal survival expert, adapting its guidance based on your speech and environmental conditions.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We used ExecuTorch for on device inference for our Edge AI solution. The model we decided on was Meta's Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct since it was small and the most practical for on device inference. To fine tune our model we used torchtune - a PyTorch library for fine tuning our Llama Model on an instance of Nvidia's H-100 using Brev.dev. We used SwiftUI for the interface on the Vision Pro and linked in binaries from ExecuTorch for implementing the on device Llama model. We used data from Terra API to simulate tracking of heartbeats and vitals which our model used to adjust its tone and focus.

sections.heading: Fine-tuning our Model
sections.text: Our Llama3.2-1B-Instruct model claimed to be fine tuned but we were a little worried when our model started generating bogus output when asked how to start a fire. We realized we needed to fine tune with 1000s of lines of code of particular scenarios our users may be in. We fine-tuned using LORA and then our custom dataset using tunetorch. We prepared them into a specific prompt/completion format using GPT-4: { "from": "human", "value": "How do I start a fire without matches? Can you please in small and concise steps explain to me how can I go about this task?" }, { "from": "assistant", "value": "1. Okay. Let us start by gathering dry tinder, such as leaves, grass, or bark. Let me know once you have got it." } Fine tuning our Llama3.2-1B model gave us much more promising results. Moving up to 3B tokens, caused our computer to crash which made us use Nvidia's Brev to fine tune with its H100 GPU.

sections.heading: What's next for SurviveX
sections.text: Using iPhone's/Vision pro's external cameras' & sensors' ability to extract video input to provide personalized feedback based off our user's point of view. Higher GPU power would possibly enable us to use a larger model on device to extend beyond the Llama3.2-1B.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Programming for the Vision Pro had limited resources and none of us had done it before. All of our team members wear glasses so they couldn't actually use the Vision Pro without switching off into contacts 😦 ExecuteTorch was only able to be run on an Intel Processor so generation of .pte files could only be done on one device. We had to stick to a smaller model such as Llama's 1B tokens because Llama3.2 with 3B slowed down on device inference. Fine tuning our model also increased the size which ran fine on MacOS and iOS but led to certain memory limits on the Vision Pro. Linking ExecuTorch and Swift within the Apple Ecosystem proved to be harder than we expected. The lack of Macbooks with an Apple Silicon chip in our team meant less hands on Swift.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: You don't need an internet connection to generate a response from an ML model! There are a lot of different survival scenarios that the wilderness can lead you to. Striking a good balance between speech-to-text and touch when developing for a hands free environment. With half of the team spending their time in the terminal we learned how useful linux commands can be.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We have never worked with on device inference or Edge AI before so it was really fulfilling to get ExecuTorch working, and generating our pte files. Fine tuning our model on our local machines proved difficult and we pivoted with Nvidia's new platform, Brev, which helped us fine tune the Llama model with higher context windows. Once we had fine tuned the model, we were able to change context length depending on the device and its capabilities. Changing the context length parameter increased the quality of the model on both the iPhone as well as the Apple Vision Pro. None of us had really built for a hands free environment like the Vision Pro before so being able to leverage Swift knowledge and connect our on device AI inference along with speech to text was a huge learning experience.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We mostly built off of the Y2K idea.

sections.heading: Why Holy XP?
sections.text: We called it holy XP after the story of the guy who single handedly made an entire OS, and made a new programming language called Holy C, slowly losing his mind in the process. We felt that we were slowly losing our minds as well while making an operating system type program, so how fitting to take some inspiration from Holy C :)

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: We simulate a real time stock exchange with gaussian distribution, we also used an additional program to display live stock market updates on a Bloomberg themed stock ticker terminal with line graphs displaying the asset prices and how they vary over time. In this game, you are a Hedge Fund manager, trying his best to stop his firm from collapsing during the hight of the 2000's dot com crash. You will receive news and possibly some insider tips via email which could be beneficial, or complete lies. It is your job to decode all the information you are given and sail your ship to safety

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: In order to work most effectively and play to each of our strengths, we divided the workload, James took control of the LLM, which would write the emails and news the payer would receive in real time. He was best suited to this task as he has experience working with local AI models in the past and during hacknotts, had spent a lot of time building a custom AI model from semi scratch. Avi was the creator of the stock market game, and the live chart system. He used tKinter to make the visuals and translated his python program into react, to more easily display it in HolyXP. He also paid close attention to the balancing of the game, at first, he realised the version he designed was far too easy, and increased the difficulty through numerous playtests and balancing asset values using mathematical models. Belal had the most experience making web apps, so we felt he was the strongest candidate to make the frontend of the app, and he used react to create a windows XP/ year 2000 themed operating system which would be the backdrop for our game. Last but definitely not least, Ilya was our main backend developer, coding the nitty gritty of the program. He worked closely with james to get the local AI model working and compatible with out program. He also assisted in designing some of the various apps/ minigames the user can play outside of the main stock market simulator.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We lost access to a remote server which was hosting the API and backend. This lead to problems with Cloudflare int he school where the WIFI would block a port that Cloudflare wanted to use. Furthermore this lead to a lot of time being thrown down the drain on the AI models, thankfully, since James had experience in this area, he was able to skilfully work out a solution and put us back on track. Another challenge we faced was the clashing programming languages, since Avi only had experience with tKinter in python, he had to spend a heavy allocation of the 24 hours learning how to translate his existing python code into react to allow his program to work simultaneously with the front end of the app. We were all exhausted with this project, working all throughout the night, notably Avi had to sleep on top of the table, which as you can imagine, wasn't the best night sleep.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of the way the GUI looks, and the seamless translation of our python app into a react enviroment. Furthermore, we pride ourselves on our lack of use of AI to code the project, and we hope the judges can appreciate a hand coded project, when especially in this day and age where many teams use AI heavily to do the thinking and coding in their project. Although our project may have bugs, and may not be the best, again, we hope you can appreciate the bugs as a natural artifact of a hand coded program, by first time hackers.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: During hacknotts, we learned how to collaborate as a team and during this process we definitely learned how to become more proficient in more languages that what we walked in with. But also how to adapt to different problems under time pressure. Additionally we loved meeting new teams and speaking to different people and learning about many new ideas and expanding all of our coding repertoire.

sections.text: Fixing the Local LLM to be more cohesive and immersive in the story.

sections.text: We wanted to make a Jarvis-like like in Iron Man, but the Desjardins sponsor challenge(and also some hardware quirks) decided to pivot to this.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our project consists of four parts: A desktop video game in which the character collects treasures and travels through various environments in which they experience a multitude of weather conditions, a mobile application that reacts to the different weather conditions that the video game character is experiencing, a shared backend server where the desktop game and banking app can communicate, and a haptic glove capable of controlling the in-game character via hand gestures as well as navigate the mobile application using voice activation and commands.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We started with the hardware, we built the glove relatively quickly, but we weren't able to DIY flex sensors(initial idea was to detect which fingers were bent for 2^5=32 possible actions) so we cut our losses & focused on aura. Linear algebra was done(Math 223 pinot the goat) with the IMU units to project ax ay az -> dx dy. Then we split our team into 2. Team A wrote the flutter mobile application, Team B built the game, and we touched base to build the server together after agreeing on the APIcontract.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Throughout the realization of this product, we encountered many ordeals that significantly impeded on the progress our team made, most of which were related to the hardware part of the project. For instance, our decision to make our very own flex sensors from scratch ended in failure and forced us to innovate and find an alternative solution. Other issues involved faulty circuitry and difficulties combining the different sections of the project.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of

Furthermore, we are very proud of our development of a server that is able to relay information between two completely different devices.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: All in all, despite the many issues we encountered in these 24 hours, we ultimately learned many lessons through our collective efforts and teamwork. We all got to pool our different skills & experiences so that by the end of the hackathon, our team had a shared understanding on electronics, fullstack dev, & the idea of "production grade code."

sections.text: We plan on continuing to develop the haptic gloves used in this project in hopes of one day helping many people such as those unable to conveniently use standard I/O devices like keyboards and mice whether it be due to working conditions or physical disabilities.

devpost_page.tagline: Arigami refolds any website into a personalised and accessible experience, making websites adapt to people, not people to websites. Controlled by gaze, voice or a switch.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Yassin, one of our group members, interacted with a family whose child has a motor-impairment disease, which made it hard for him to be independent; his disability limited him from completing any tasks or learning on his own, a story which inspired our team to create Arigami.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Arigami is a Chrome/Edge extension that replaces the webpage you're on with a redesign that fits your accessibility needs in 1 of 3 tracks: Focus, Motor impairment, or Screen reader. It maintains a given website's look and content, and and an optional AI redesign uses Apify and Claude to read the website and reorganize the page.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We researched into existing products, seeing what gaze trackers and accessibility extensions already exist based on our initial idea. From there, we prototyped different designs in Figma and used Claude to code.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Being unable to design a model that relies purely on one's eye movements within the Hackathon timeframe, leading us to create a model that tracks one's gaze instead Using new tools for the first time, such as Figma and Apify No way to test our model on actual motor impairment cases, having to work only with research and personal experiences with motor impaired individuals Learning to create a Chrome extension for the first time

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: One feature that we're proud of is having our product be able to remodel webpages based on one's specific accessibility needs while maintaining the integrity of the website. For motor impaired individuals, this includes enlarged buttons with more spacing, and buttons that group features on a website, allowing them to access different parts with ease. Designing the scrolling gradient was also a part of our project we were proud of, at it immediately made the extension feel much more accessible. Before that, the user would look at the "Scroll down" and "Scroll up" buttons, which would only scroll at one set speed. The head tracking design feels very seamless while your using it, and we were very proud of the ease of navigation it created during our own testing of the product.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Firstly, we learned how to integrate different software into our design process to promote collaborative thought and efficiency, such as Figma. We learned that the most technically complex project may not always be the most helpful project, and that there are many meaningful ways an impact can be made. As such, we learned how to prioritize what we thought was most important to work on to reach our desired product. For example, we did not add a voice agent because it is likely someone who is blind already has one, which may cause more issues for them rather than less if Arigami also had one. Our team has never competed at CalHacks before, so managing the time pressure and intensity of the event was something we needed to work to adjust to, as well, figuring out what worked best for us in this new environment.

sections.heading: What's next for Arigami
sections.text: Next, we want to build out Arigami further, validating its use in real world applications. We would want to test it and discuss with people who have accessibility needs to continue getting feedback and improving. We want to eventually make our product fully fit into Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and continuing to optimize our UI.
